title: Resources
text:
All labs use STATA on your own laptop. Stata 17 or later is required (xtdidregress, used in Session 4, was introduced in Stata 17).


Please install the following packages before the first session. Run the block once from the Stata command window or a do-file:
* Session 1 — sensitivity analysis
ssc install sensemakr, replace

* Session 3 — randomization inference
ssc install ritest, replace

* Session 4 — heterogeneity-robust DiD and event-study plots
ssc install drdid, replace
ssc install csdid, replace
ssc install did_imputation, replace
ssc install event_plot, replace

* Session 5 — additional IV diagnostics
ssc install ranktest, replace
ssc install ivreg2, replace
If ssc install fails on the university network, try again from a different connection or download the package files from SSC and install them with net install.



Assignments and the final paper must be accompanied by a do-file that reproduces all results. A minimal structure:
* ------------------------------------------------------------
* Project:  <title>
* Author:   <name>
* Date:     <date>
* Purpose:  reproduces all tables and figures in the paper
* ------------------------------------------------------------
version 18
clear all
set more off
set seed 20262027

* Paths: change only this line
global root "C:/Users/<you>/qmm2627_assignment1"

use "$root/data/mydata.dta", clear

* 1. Data preparation
* 2. Descriptives
* 3. Main models
* 4. Robustness and diagnostics
Set version to the Stata version you use, always set a seed when results depend on randomization (bootstrap, randomization inference, matching with ties), and never hard-code paths inside the analysis.

title: Luiss Guido Carli | PhD in Politics | Quantitative Methods Masterclass
text:
Programme
PhD in Politics — second year


Period
First semester, 2026-2027


Instructor
Francesco Visconti


Field
Methods of Political Research


Software
STATA (on your own laptop)

title: Luiss Guido Carli | PhD in Politics | Quantitative Methods Masterclass
Luiss Guido Carli | PhD in Politics | Quantitative Methods Masterclass
text:
Applying knowledge and understanding
Students will be able to understand advanced quantitative methods relevant to their doctoral dissertations or research projects, and to specify, estimate, diagnose and interpret in STATA a measurement model, a difference-in-differences design and an instrumental variables estimation, reporting the results according to disciplinary standards.

title: Luiss Guido Carli | PhD in Politics | Quantitative Methods Masterclass
text:
Making judgements
Through the discussion of published applications and replications, students will learn to assess the credibility of others’ identifying assumptions and to choose knowingly the analytical strategy best suited to their own research question, recognising when the available data do not support a causal answer.

title: Luiss Guido Carli | PhD in Politics | Quantitative Methods Masterclass
text:
Communication skills
Students will improve their ability to present and discuss the results of their quantitative analyses, refining oral and written communication skills with particular attention to clarity and accuracy in data presentation.

title: Luiss Guido Carli | PhD in Politics | Quantitative Methods Masterclass
text:
Learning skills
The course fosters autonomy in methodological updating, training students to read recent methodological literature, to consult software documentation and to work with replicable code.

title: Sessions
text:
Readings marked as Optional are for further study and are not required for class discussion. Slides, do-files and data are added to each session as the course progresses.


Session 1 — Beyond control variables
Regression, identification and selection on observables

What a regression coefficient actually estimates. From “controlling for” to identification: omitted variable bias in explicit form, DAGs as a tool for choosing controls, good and bad controls (colliders, mediators, post-treatment bias). Alternatives to regression under selection on observables: matching, weighting (IPW), doubly robust estimation. What we can say when ignorability is not credible: sensitivity analysis.




Materials
Slides, do-file and data will be posted here.





Readings

Keele, L., Stevenson, R. T., & Elwert, F. (2020). The Causal Interpretation of Estimated Associations in Regression Models. Political Science Research and Methods, 8(1), 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1017/psrm.2019.31
Huntington-Klein, N. (2022). The Effect: An Introduction to Research Design and Causality. CRC Press, chs. 5, 8 and 13. Open access: https://theeffectbook.net



Optional readings

Cinelli, C., & Hazlett, C. (2020). Making Sense of Sensitivity: Extending Omitted Variable Bias. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B, 82(1), 39–67. https://doi.org/10.1111/rssb.12348
Montgomery, J. M., Nyhan, B., & Torres, M. (2018). How Conditioning on Posttreatment Variables Can Ruin Your Experiment and What to Do About It. American Journal of Political Science, 62(3), 760–775. https://doi.org/10.1111/ajps.12357




Session 2 — Measuring concepts
From exploratory factor analysis to CFA, SEM and measurement equivalence

Measurement error and its consequences for regression estimates. From the exploratory factor analysis covered in the first year to the confirmatory model: specification, identification, fit indices, modification indices and the risk of specification search. Structural equation models with latent variables. The central problem of comparative research: measurement equivalence across countries and over time (configural, metric and scalar invariance), and what to do when it does not hold.






–>  –>  –>








Session 3 — The experimental benchmark
Experiments, survey experiments and conjoint designs

Randomization as the solution to the identification problem: what changes, in a regression, when treatment is assigned by the researcher. Laboratory, field and survey experiments. The main survey-experimental designs in research on public opinion and electoral behavior: vignette, framing, priming, list and endorsement experiments. Conjoint designs: profile randomization, AMCEs and marginal means, and the assumptions that underpin them (stability, no carryover or order effects, the distribution of attributes). Subgroup analysis and effect heterogeneity: interactions, marginal effects, and the most common errors in their specification and interpretation. Statistical power, pre-registration, multiple comparisons. Demand effects, non-probability samples and external validity.






–>  –>  –>










Session 4 — From fixed effects to difference-in-differences
DiD, parallel trends, staggered adoption

DiD as a natural extension of the panel models students already know, and as an attempt to reconstruct the counterfactual that an experiment guarantees by design. The parallel trends assumption: what it implies, how it can be argued for, and why it cannot be tested directly. Event-study specifications and pre-trends. The problem with two-way fixed effects under staggered treatment adoption and heterogeneous effects: negative weights and “bad” comparisons. Heterogeneity-robust estimators. A brief introduction to synthetic control.






–>  –>  –>









Session 5 — Instrumental variables
Endogeneity, relevance, exclusion

Endogeneity as a structural problem and the logic of two-stage least squares. The three assumptions (relevance, exclusion, monotonicity) and their epistemic status: two of them can be defended only through argument. What an instrument actually estimates: the LATE, compliers, and the problem of the target population, with an explicit return to the effect heterogeneity discussed in Session 3. Weak instruments and finite-sample bias. A critical review of the instruments most widely used in political science (weather, historical instruments, shift-share) and of the critiques they have attracted. Experimental encouragement designs and regression discontinuity as special cases.






–>  –>  –>








Session 6 — From numbers to cases
Multi-method research, mechanisms and transparency

The inherent limits of the quantitative toolkit: what a well-identified estimate still cannot tell us. Nested analysis as a research architecture. Case selection following a statistical analysis: typical, deviant and influential cases, and the logic behind the choice. Process tracing as a tool for investigating mechanisms. Qualitative evidence in support of measurement validity (returning to Session 2), the interpretation of experimental treatments (Session 3), and arguments about identifying assumptions (Sessions 4 and 5). Quant–qual and qual–quant sequences. Transparency, replicability and open data.
The session includes a workshop in which students present the design of their final paper.






–>  –>  –>

title: Assessment
text:
Attendance and active participation are required. In case of justified absence, please inform the instructor in advance.
The final grade is expressed in thirtieths (/30). The pass mark is 18/30 and the maximum grade is 30/30 cum laude.








Component
Weight
Covers




Participation
10%
All sessions


Assignment 1 — Measure and control
20%
Sessions 1–2


Assignment 2 — Replicate and assess
20%
Sessions 3–5


Final paper
50%
One method of the course applied to your own research




Participation (10%)
Attendance and active engagement in class discussions. Come to class having read the required readings for the session.


Assignments (40%, 20% each)
Two papers of 1,000 words max, each accompanied by a do-file that fully reproduces the results.

Measure and control (Sessions 1–2).
Replicate and assess (Sessions 3–5).

Assignments are assessed on the correctness of the analysis, the quality of the justification of choices, the reproducibility of the code and the clarity of presentation.



Final paper (50%)
A methodological paper of up to 3,000 words in which students apply one of the course methods to their own doctoral research question. The paper must:

motivate the choice of design;
state the identifying assumptions;
discuss their plausibility in the student’s case.

Reproducibility is also assessed: the paper must be accompanied by code and data, or by instructions for obtaining them. Students present the design of their final paper in the workshop held during Session 6.
